analysis.one_liner: Expands a protected Oregon watershed that supplies Portland's drinking water and bans logging there.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned timber cutting across a 98,272-acre watershed and added land to it, was introduced in September 1998 and died in House subcommittees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have enlarged the Bull Run Watershed Management Unit in Oregon — the forested area that supplies Portland's drinking water — to about 98,272 acres and banned tree cutting on all federal land inside it. It would also have repealed two 1996 laws that had allowed some management flexibility in parts of the unit, and directed the Forest Service to negotiate a land swap giving the city of Portland title to the federal land under its Bull Run water facilities in exchange for city-owned forest land.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the Portland area, who drink water drawn from the Bull Run watershed, would gain stronger protection for that water supply: logging across the entire unit would be prohibited rather than allowed in parts of it, and two 1996 laws that had opened the door to more flexible management would be repealed [S2] [S3]. The city of Portland would also gain a path to own the federal land under its Bull Run water facilities through a congressionally directed land exchange, with a deadline of September 30, 2001 [S2] [S3]. Fish and wildlife habitat and forest recreation in the Little Sandy River watershed would gain from the added protections [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Portland-area water drinkers and watershed supporters

how_it_helps.text: Bans tree cutting on all federal land in the expanded Bull Run unit, removing the logging exception that 1996 law had created for parts of the unit outside the Bull Run River drainage [S2] [S3].
Adds the Little Sandy River watershed to the protected unit, enlarging it to roughly 98,272 acres [S2] [S3].

Directs the Secretary of Agriculture to negotiate, at Portland's request, a land exchange transferring the national forest land under the city's Bull Run water facilities to the city within roughly three years, giving the city direct control of the ground its water system sits on [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which would lose the ability to log federal land in the unit: the bill repeals the 1996 Oregon Resource Conservation Act provision requiring lands outside the Bull Run River drainage to be managed under the unit's law and repeals a duplicative 1996 parks law section, while requiring the Secretary to prohibit cutting trees on federal land across the entire enlarged unit [S2] [S3]. The federal government would also give up title to the land under Portland's water facilities in the exchange, receiving city-owned land inside national forests in return [S2] [S3]. The bill states it has no effect on anyone's water rights [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The timber industry, which would lose the logging

drawbacks.text: Ending timber harvest on the entire enlarged unit would permanently remove federal forest land there from logging, which the timber industry and affected timber-dependent communities would bear as lost harvest opportunity; the bill sets no compensation or transition for that loss [S2] [S3].

The land exchange would give a city permanent ownership of federal land, bypassing the normal rule that swapped parcels must be in the same state — the bill expressly waives that same-state limit to let Portland offer land in either Oregon or Washington [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — protecting the drinking-water source for the Portland area and halting logging in the watershed — is significant and permanent, while the main cost falls on a specific industry's access to this particular federal forest. The land-exchange provision is the part most open to debate, since it directs a federal-to-city title transfer on an expedited timetable, though it would follow normal exchange law otherwise and the bill takes no position on existing water rights [S2] [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of the session, sent to two House committees, and sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on September 9, 1998, with Reps. Elizabeth Furse and Darlene Hooley of Oregon signed on, late in the second session of the 105th Congress [S1] [S3].

The Speaker sent it to both the Resources and Agriculture committees; it was referred to the Forests and Forest Health and National Parks and Public Lands subcommittees, and executive comment was requested from the Agriculture and Interior Departments on September 15, 1998 [S1] [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the action record ends at the subcommittee referrals, and the 105th Congress adjourned on January 3, 1999 with the bill still in committee [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one's drinking water gained new protection and no logging was barred, because the bill never advanced. Timber access in the watershed was unchanged by this bill, and the status quo its sponsors wanted to overturn simply carried forward.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo: unchanged logging rules in the watershed

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the House.

for.name: Reps. Elizabeth Furse and Darlene Hooley
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees and their subcommittees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 9, 1998 and referred it to subcommittees, but held no hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded supporters were three Oregon House Democrats, and no recorded opposition appears in the action history.

industries.note: The bill would have banned tree cutting across the entire 98,272-acre unit and repealed the 1996 provision that allowed different management on unit lands outside the Bull Run River drainage, ending logging opportunity in the watershed. The record shows no action on the bill, so the industry's access there was never actually changed by it.

The bill directed negotiations to transfer the federal land under Portland's Bull Run water facilities to the city, and its protections would safeguard the source of the city's drinking water. The city's interest and its residents' water supply run together here.
